items.question: How do you see humanoid robots fitting into the future of human development?
items.object: Humanoid robots and the future of human development
items.answer: I see human development as a process of continually eliminating our own flesh-and-blood bodies. Ten years from now, I would not be at all surprised to see a humanoid robot pick up water and drink it while working outdoors. Once we collectively break through all the technologies, this will certainly be a market worth hundreds of billions or trillions.

items.question: Why do you see value in building your startup’s teams in both Shenzhen and Silicon Valley?
items.object: Building teams in both Shenzhen and Silicon Valley
items.answer: Given my own experience, I have a relatively more comprehensive understanding than others of the engineers and industrial development on both sides. I think every place has its advantages. Silicon Valley, I feel, has for a long time, and still does, had a culture of not fearing failure, encouraging innovation, and encouraging mobility of people. People working there are often very active-minded and active in applying and exploring new technologies. China, I think, has advantages of its own in many respects. In the past two years, the country has also been encouraging innovation and technological breakthroughs more. But in many respects, I think it still lacks a bit of the Silicon Valley spirit. That is not a problem, because China's industry has developed major advantages over Silicon Valley of its own, especially in supply chains. So I think both places have their strengths and weaknesses. Creating teams in both places and bringing together people from different places, backgrounds, and ways of thinking into one team is very necessary in this era.

items.question: How do you explain why humanoid robots have not yet reached the reliability standards DJI set for its drones?
items.object: Humanoid robot reliability and the development of DJI drones
items.answer: I think we can analyze this through the objective laws governing how things develop. The first time I saw a drone was probably in 2009, in the Indian film 3 Idiots. There was a scene that left a deep impression on me: a student was constantly neglecting his proper studies to make his own little inventions. What did he invent? A quadrotor drone. But because he was doing this, his grades were poor, and the teacher threatened to expel him. Eventually he could not take it anymore and committed suicide. When he did, the protagonist of the film helped tune the student's aircraft and added a video link, a remote-control video link. He flew it up to surprise the student, only to discover, through the drone's view, that he had already hanged himself in his dormitory. That was in 2009. In fact, by 2009 drones had already been developing for nearly a decade. So at that point, the idea of a remotely controlled aircraft with video transmission, though still new, could already be depicted in a film. People could see it and think, oh, this is useful, this has value. But DJI did not truly begin saying that Boeing should be its competitor until 2014 or 2015. At that point DJI had launched Phantom 1 in early 2013 and achieved a fairly large sales volume. Then, after large numbers of users began using it and accidents occurred, we had to reduce the failure rate. We had to hold drone systems to the standards of aerospace and aviation systems. That was when such a reliability target was proposed. If you imagine selling one million, even two million, aircraft flying all over the sky, a failure rate of one in two million would still mean quite a lot of failures. That is why there was such a requirement, or goal. But from 2009, when the drone technology was mature, to 2013, when DJI found the use case of a flying camera, there were... Four years. Then from DJI getting started to discovering, after major sales, that products needed reliability requirements, several more years passed. So humanoid robots today are like drones in 2009. I think perhaps they are not even there yet; perhaps they are earlier still. Many foundational technologies have not yet been studied clearly. At this point, many things are research-oriented. Of course, because we have experience with many other electromechanical systems, especially drones, we can roughly foresee that within two years, commercially oriented consumer-category robots should emerge. They will certainly have drone-like requirements for reliability, mass production, quality, and so on, so we can make some projections. But at this point, is it a fully mature thing? In my view, it is not. Yet perhaps all that is missing is some commercial companies aiming at large-scale mass production and painstakingly working through every detail. If we do not do this, the future in which they can be mass-produced and stable certainly will not arrive, right? Doing it carries the risk of failure, but it is still better than not doing it.

items.question: Why do you think Tesla is closest to Boeing-level reliability among today’s humanoid and general-purpose robotics companies?
items.object: Tesla’s prospects for achieving Boeing-level reliability in robotics
items.answer: I think it is still Tesla. This is public; people have discussed it through public channels. For robots today, many parts of the system—from deployment to hardware to data collection and testing—still inherit infrastructure that Tesla's automotive business line has already built. So if Tesla really makes 5,000 robots this year, wherever they are deployed, Tesla has a very complete existing system and process for collecting and analyzing their failures. Most startups certainly have many people who have never done this kind of thing; right now, perhaps everyone is still figuring out how to make the technology solid. Making the technology solid is the first step. The second is how to mass-produce it. And mass production is not the whole picture; another part is after-sales service: once users receive it, will it have problems frequently? Then there is another part: repair returns. A user may wear the thing out, or after some time the whole system's performance may decline. Does it need to be taken back to some repair center for maintenance, or mailed to some return-repair service location run by the company? So there are actually many stages in between that people may not have paid much attention to.

items.question: How do you understand DJI’s approach to technology as a former early employee and now a consumer?
items.object: DJI’s approach to technology and user experience
items.answer: I have been away from DJI for a long time, so honestly I do not know much about the company's strategy or thinking. I can only say that, as a very early employee and now an ordinary consumer, my view is that technology is not about saying, “If I start a company, I must realize some especially, especially leading technology.” More often, it is about analyzing user needs, combining different technologies to deliver a great user experience, and creating new productivity. items.question: How do you judge whether a humanoid robot is the right tool for a particular user need?
items.object: Humanoid robots as tools for meeting user needs
items.answer: Maybe users will say, “I do not just need an OSMO; I need a solution that can hold the OSMO for me and follow me around.” Now, as robotics researchers and practitioners, we might think, “Oh, a humanoid robot that carries your camera is a very good solution.” But whether that is the best user experience is not certain. Maybe you make a vehicle, or just a lower body, or something like RONIN—an additional stabilization device attached to a person. From DJI's perspective, I think all those solutions are the same, because the experience they ultimately provide for image capture may be the same. A humanoid robot is only one possible tool for solving a particular user need. This tool has strengths and weaknesses. Often, you cannot simply say, “I must use it”; rather, you need to ask how to solve the problem well. It is like the saying: are you holding a hammer and looking for nails? Or do you see a nail and then choose the appropriate hammer? In my view, humanoid robots are potentially very capable hammers—perhaps more like Swiss Army knives. They can certainly do many, many things, but in many situations you may just need a simple, ordinary hammer. In my view, many user scenarios need a simple hammer rather than a complex Swiss Army knife.

items.question: How do you view the prospects for humanoid robots given their current limitations and the availability of simpler tools?
items.object: The current limitations and future value of humanoid robots
items.answer: Oh, I do not see it as unpromising. I think it is simply an inevitable stage in how things develop. Humanoid robots will certainly have more complete functionality, better stability, more degrees of freedom, and be able to solve more problems. But right now, simply, the hardware technology is immature, so they are expensive; the software technology is immature, so they are not smart enough. If we get all those things right, they will certainly create great value. But they will not eliminate hammers, and hammers will not leave them with little room to be useful. As tools, I think both will have great reason to exist in large numbers.

items.question: How do you see the long-term development of humanoid robotics?
items.object: The long-term development of humanoid robotics
items.answer: In 2018—perhaps earlier than that—humanoid robotics was a problem that had not been well solved in research. Of course, looking now, there are indeed a great many research and engineering problems to solve, so I wanted to study it. At the time, there were not many mature humanoid approaches; robot dogs were still the main thing. I cannot say I foresaw the field becoming as hot as it is now, but I believed it was useful. Still, I was not blindly optimistic that it would have broad applications within one or two years, as we were just discussing. I think it is necessarily a long-term, ongoing process. Looking at humanoid robots alone, over the past fifty years they have come in waves. In the 1980s, Japanese scientists produced some approaches; then around 2000, ASIMO was made, something that astonished the world. After that, people made many small consumer humanoid robots, but none was very successful. I feel that this wave, conservatively speaking, will certainly be bigger than those, but it will also certainly have ups and downs. We are sure that the technologies we have today have made a lot of progress compared with the previous generation's technologies. But I do not believe they are enough to solve every household scenario we imagine. So I think we can do a bit better than they did, but we are still far from our dream. Very likely, we will need wave after wave of product exploration.

items.question: How do you think humanoid robots could overcome the heat problems that limit their ability to work outdoors?
items.object: Heat dissipation as a constraint on outdoor humanoid robots
items.answer: Technically, I think there is still room for breakthroughs in materials. For example, with today's motors, no matter how you build them, they still cannot guarantee stable operation under all working conditions. If a robot is outdoors in very hot weather, whether it is a Unitree robot or a Tesla robot, it will have overheating problems. How do we solve that? I think it is a materials problem. For example, perhaps we will have new materials for the conductors inside motors, improving heat generation and resistance characteristics and thus system stability. Or perhaps we will have new motor designs so that, say, the robot can have a water tank inside it with some water. It could move the water to the motors itself and cool them through something like sweating or evaporation, improving their operating conditions. None of that is certain. We do not currently have very mature technologies to do this. But you can imagine that perhaps in five years—again, five years—or ten years... Ten years from now, I would not be at all surprised to see a humanoid robot pick up water and drink it while working outdoors, because it needs to dissipate heat. Because no matter how efficient a motor is, it will still generate heat; that is a law of physics. So how does it dissipate heat? It can only drink water and evaporate it. Cars have coolant too. So, speaking only of the technology that would support robots working continuously outdoors in high temperatures, we do not currently possess it. That may limit many application scenarios for robot systems that can be built today. Once the technology is solved, robots' application scenarios may expand.

items.question: How do you see product iteration and technological breakthroughs working together to advance robotics?
items.object: Product iteration and technological breakthroughs in robotics
items.answer: I think both are needed. Generation after generation of product and hardware iteration is simply about finding an application scenario and building it; if there is a problem, seeing whether new technology can be added to expand its operating and business scope. This process will necessarily ebb and flow. Maybe today there is a mechanical innovation, tomorrow a hardware innovation, and the day after an algorithmic innovation, allowing us to iterate generation by generation toward products with better functionality and more stable performance. But as for whether there will be a moment when we suddenly build a robot system smarter than humans that can do this and that—my personal feeling is that it will not appear all at once. Over a long period in the future, we will see product A, product B, product C, and a process of gradual improvement.

items.question: Why did you change your view that students should stop researching quadrotors?
items.object: Quadrotors as research platforms
items.answer: I think that judgment of mine was wrong. Before doing my PhD, I did not understand especially clearly what was an engineering problem and what was a research problem. Saying people should not research quadrotors was actually purely engineering thinking: we already understood very clearly how to build the thing. But from a research perspective, as I understand now, it is still an excellent research platform. It is small, can fly quickly, and can move flexibly in the air. For research in navigation and path planning, it is a very good platform for implementing and validating algorithms. And precisely because many of its engineering problems have been worked out clearly, researchers do not need to think about foundational issues such as how to assemble the drone hardware or design basic low-level control algorithms. So my judgment was incorrect. Or rather, it took me a long time to understand clearly what engineering is and what science is.

items.question: How do you understand the distinction between engineering and science in robotics PhD work?
items.object: The distinction between engineering and science in robotics PhD research
items.answer: Later I saw a quote from von Kármán—he was probably Qian Xuesen's professor—about what engineering and science are, or what scientists and engineers do. He said scientists explain what already exists. And engineers create things that do not exist. So PhD work should really explain what already exists, or explain science. For example, if you have an aircraft that flies poorly with method A but very well with method B—it can avoid obstacles and be more stable—then scientifically you need to explain why. Say it uses a neural-network method: why does using a neural-network method make it better? How can you make it better still? Are the relevant factors the network architecture, the training method, or something else? Scientists should do more of this part. It is just that robotics as a whole is still not very mature, so PhD students often first need to do engineering, build a platform themselves, and then conduct research on it and explain the scientific part. Before my own PhD, I may have thought PhD work was the engineering part, creating unknown things. But after completing it, I found it was not like that: PhD work should explain known things. Of course, there are subtle distinctions here. Often you need to create something first and then explain the science behind it. Or, on very short timescales, you have to alternate between the two.

items.question: Where do you think the main gap lies between research work and an actual hardware product?
items.object: The gap between research and a finished hardware product
items.answer: I have no doubt that the distance is large. But the main gap is not the technology itself; it is how the technology, once it enters a product, fits into the process from technical implementation to mass production, after-sales service, and return repair. For hardware products, every one of these is crucial. Technology may appear in every part of that, and there may still be science in it. But solving it is more often a systemic matter: you must have people responsible for return repair and after-sales service, collect data, and analyze it. Everyone says all companies have to do these things, but in practice there are many fragmented issues that need attention.

items.question: How do you understand the continuing value of traditional control theory and system modeling in reinforcement learning?
items.object: The continuing value of control theory and system modeling in reinforcement learning
items.answer: I talked with Professor Zhang Wei of Southern University of Science and Technology the year before last, and he inspired me greatly. I have always admired him; he is a scholar with a very traditional control-theory background. He had taught at Ohio State, and his classes were very hardcore: Lyapunov stability, state-space models, and very traditional, rigorous mathematical control theory. But after becoming a professor at SUSTech, and later founding Zhujidongli, much of his work moved quickly into reinforcement learning. Once, over dinner, I asked him whether he felt that all his accumulated work from so many years had been wasted. He did not, because he believes reinforcement learning is very model-based. Why? Much of the progress in reinforcement learning now comes from NVIDIA bringing physical simulation onto GPUs, and physical simulation is an extremely model-based approach, and extremely optimization-based. You construct the system's kinematics and solve it; along the way this involves Euler methods, estimation, and handling contact constraints. People doing model predictive control, robotics, and physical simulation are basically all working in the same line of thought and framework. So no matter how reinforcement-learning algorithms or training frameworks evolve today, when you simulate contact forces, you still have to transform very complex constraints into something like linear complementarity constraints and solve them. Those things do not change. No matter how you optimize a simulator, you still have to begin from those fundamental physical properties. From this perspective, he says that all the knowledge of control theory and system modeling will continue to apply very well to simulation. People's understanding of models is embedded in simulators. Meanwhile, reinforcement-learning neural networks are simply implicitly learning into the network people's understanding of physics that is in the simulator. So he does not think earlier knowledge gets wasted or anything like that.

items.question: How do you understand Elon Musk's approach to meetings with engineers at Tesla Optimus?

When someone presents slides, he looks very carefully at the presenter and follows the whole process very attentively. Usually he does not ask extremely detailed questions. items.question: How do you understand the sense of mission shared by DJI and Tesla?
items.object: DJI and Tesla’s shared sense of mission
items.answer: I think what they have in common is that DJI and Tesla are both in a position within their industries of saying, “I must make something new.” Drones were inherently a very new thing for DJI. items.question: How close do you think we are to a human-sized robot that can do useful household chores?
items.object: The development of useful household humanoid robots
items.answer: I think that, certainly, within three to five years, a complete solution—a human-sized robot that can do some useful household chores—will definitely appear. These functions have all been demonstrated. It is of course still many steps away from truly being for the home. But it seems we have already carved the metal into a usable hardware system. items.question: How do you see humanoid robots fitting alongside other robot forms in people's homes?
items.object: Humanoid robots and alternative robot forms in the home
items.answer: In the long run, wheeled robots, humanoid robots, other forms, even drones, even robotic arms hanging from ceilings—these will all exist, and all have their own application scenarios and value. Humanoid robots are of course the coolest direction of research at this moment, but once they mature, they will simply be one thing in people's toolbox, like robotic arms, wheels, and other mechanical forms. I do believe humanoid robots will be one of the best solutions, but in terms of entering people's lives and freeing them from everyday work, solutions may take many forms. In the future, a home may have, for example, a wheeled cooking robot in the first-floor kitchen area, and another humanoid robot for household organization, because it may need to gather things on the first floor and carry them upstairs. Many homes in Europe and America are basically two-story homes, especially in the United States. Wheeled robots cannot climb stairs. But once a robot carries clothes and so on upstairs into the laundry room, that laundry room may have a single- or dual-arm robot suspended from the ceiling. It can hang down over a table, put things into the washing machine, take them out, and fold them. It may not need wheels at all, or even need to move. It only needs to move within a small area on the laundry-room ceiling.

items.question: Do you expect household robots to become capable of clearing the table after a hot-pot meal within five or ten years?
items.object: The gradual development and commercialization of household robots
items.answer: I do not think so. I think it will necessarily be progressive. Perhaps over the next few years, what will gradually happen is that a company comes forward and says, “Our solution can pick up any object you drop on the floor and put it into a specific box.” Through certain commercial trade-offs, perhaps you only have to pay one or two thousand dollars for it. For example, many robot-vacuum companies now add robotic arms to vacuums. But the vacuum's form is necessarily limited, so many tasks are beyond its coverage. That will further lead people to think: oh, a vacuum plus an arm can solve many problems; if we add eyes and continue iterating on that basis, it can certainly solve more problems, and people will be willing to pay for it. I think scenarios will be uncovered gradually, and people will gradually iterate more suitable hardware to solve them. At first it may not be a complete solution that sounds especially sexy. But it is the same: over the next five years, capability will advance gradually. items.question: How do you view the convergence of humanoid robotics companies toward similar technical approaches?
items.object: Technological convergence and product differentiation in humanoid robotics
items.answer: My view is that technological convergence is normal, because mature technologies are technologies that can be applied at scale. items.answer: That is possible. But there are a few points. Returning to the car example, assembly-line technology was a very important beginning of cars' large-scale adoption. Yet before Ford made automotive assembly lines, Mercedes, BMW, and others were already making cars, and there were certainly many technical differences among them. But once assembly lines became widespread, everyone could follow. When many technical approaches are indeed similar, it is also easy to apply and learn from technologies developed by others. So the auto industry did not end up with one company making a technical breakthrough and all the others dying. That does not happen. And if the ecosystem has some companies specializing in hardware and some in software, software companies can adjust fairly flexibly. Hardware companies can choose the most suitable partners and adjust actively and quickly as well. That is okay too. I think this is more a matter of organizational management.

items.question: Where do you think a startup's real moat comes from when technological knowledge is widely shared?
items.object: Startup moats when technological knowledge is widely shared
items.answer: Many fields now show this state: technological moats that once seemed as though they could be deeply hidden suddenly get disrupted by new deep-learning and model-based methods. And these technologies are shared in academia, so many technological moats do not sound that deep. This returns to organizational management. The entire team must work through more details: details of model training, deployment, hardware and software, and so on. Getting those details right, and accumulating them, creates enormous differences and a moat. Again, take DJI. In my view, DJI's technological moat is its pursuit of every detail. Twelve years have passed since DJI made the Phantom. The industry has very mature solutions for drone flight control, camera tuning, and image transmission, but when others put them together, their products are simply not as good as DJI's. Still, we can see certain points others may overlook or fail to focus on.

items.question: If you were an investor, what kind of robotics startup would you want to invest in?
items.object: Investing in robotics startups developing foundational technologies
items.answer: Personally, I might focus on longer-term problems. By long-term, I mean foundational technologies—for example, the humanoid robot drinking water that I just mentioned and using evaporation. To me, that is a key foundational technology, perhaps directly related to motors. Or could motor materials or something else be different? I would care more about whether, on a long timescale, some component of a robot can reach the human level or embody a human-like approach. So if a company came along and said, “We have a motor solution that achieves that,” I would consider it important. Even if the technology could not be used on a particular humanoid robot within five years, I would think it had long-term value. Of course, from the standpoint of investment returns, as an investor we would ask whether it could sell a joint motor to current humanoid-robot makers in the meantime, or make some smaller existing motor categories—other commercially deployable projects. But I might invest because it could in the long run make something more human-like or solve a breakthrough technology point, while allowing it to conduct some commercial exploration in the short term. From my perspective, it must prove itself commercially. So that it can do longer-term things. Because, as we just said, with foundation models, you might invest one hundred million for fifteen years and still not have enough. You may need several investors, each investing one hundred million, for fifteen years.

items.question: How do you understand increasingly capable robots as part of humanity’s own development?
items.object: Human history as the joint evolution of humans and machines
items.answer:
In my view, the development of human history itself is a process of humans and robots developing together. Because if you broaden the definition of robots, then all the tools humans have made, all electromechanical systems—their gradual development is somewhat like a process of biological evolution. At the very beginning there were single-celled organisms—a stick, or a stone flake. Then people might bind a stick and a stone together to make an axe. Later, they made wheels from wood, and plows for tilling land from iron. Later, they built houses, made household tools, and gradually there were clocks, more complex equipment, printers, typewriters, then airplanes, cars, and trains. These, little by little, are all an evolution of tools, up to today’s robots.

And humans are not something that exists alone. Before tools, humans were the same as monkeys. It was only after humans emerged that there were tools—or rather, it was tools that distinguished us from monkeys. So the history of the evolution of machines is actually a definition of us as humans—of humanity itself. When we say that human history has developed and improved, it is not actually that humans themselves have undergone some kind of evolution; rather, it is that the machines humans make have gotten better and better. From this perspective, improvements in the capabilities and intelligence of the robots we create are precisely a symbol of improved capability and intelligence for the human species.

And from a more long-term perspective, when each of us is freed from complicated, trivial household chores, humanity will certainly gain more productivity, because our minds can be used to think about more things, and our lives will get better. Then we should make our living spaces and the robots we create more intelligent, smarter, more creative. And in the long run, the two will certainly coexist.

items.question: Why do you think a future civilization of humans in machine bodies would still be human civilization?
items.object: Humanity’s long-term transition from biological bodies to a machine civilization
items.answer:
Perhaps in a few thousand years, the human fleshly body may disappear—that is, our consciousness will transfer into machine bodies—but the human species will still exist. Because from today’s perspective, human development is actually a process of continually eliminating our own fleshly bodies, or, put another way, of continually severing ourselves from nature. So the direction of human evolution is a process of becoming mechanized.

This question has gone a bit far into the future, but let me tell you something very basic: this human instinct—how to put it—say you go to a hotel, get into a bathtub, and find a strand of hair in it. You think, ah, that’s disgusting; it’s something left by the previous person. Humans actually have an instinctive disgust toward human fleshly bodies and their excretions. But if you went into that hotel, got into a bathtub, and found a piece of wire there, you’d think, oh, whatever, maybe it’s something from the renovation or something; I’ll just throw it away. You wouldn’t think it was dirty. But could it be that the previous tenant—the previous hotel guest—was a robot? In this scenario, if the previous tenant was a human, that makes you feel disgusted; but if the previous tenant was a robot, that makes you feel close to it.

So something deeply rooted in human nature is the pursuit of the elimination of our own flesh, and of achieving a better connection with machines. Of course, that is a question humans thousands of years from now will need to think about. But I think the state human society will develop toward is further de-bodification of humans because of these questions, making us all into a purely machine civilization. But it would still be human civilization, because from the beginning, human civilization has been bound together with machine civilization; the two are one.

For me, for us contemporary humans, you can’t survive without machines around you. Our food, drinking water, much of our transportation, clothing, food, housing, and travel are all provided by machines now. To a certain extent, we already coexist symbiotically with machines. items.question: Why do you think a future machine society might need to impose death on digital life?
items.object: Mortality and creativity in a future machine society
items.answer: I think a future machine society will need to discuss, over the long term, whether digital life should be allowed to die. That is, I think humans, as entities that coexist symbiotically with machines, will continue our state and way of life. It will continue indefinitely. But machines will then begin to need to discuss whether they should enter the human mode and way of life. The biggest point there is whether digital information and consciousness need to be actively erased and eliminated. Because a robot can keep copying its own memory, as well as its experiences and its data. A robot and its consciousness can be said to be immortal; it can move around among different servers throughout the world. So what a machine-dominated society will need to think about in the future is whether it needs to impose, on citizens in that society, death in the physical sense, including destruction of the body and the consciousness of a robot stored on the internet. Otherwise, without the threat of death, robots cannot achieve human creativity.” This is a very, very unusual view of mine.

items.question: Why do you think a future machine society might need to give each machine life a finite lifespan?
items.object: Mortality as a source of creativity and a possible requirement for machine life
items.answer: For us humans—any human behavior, because it has to face death, this greatly determines the way a person speaks, acts, and lives. Once you no longer fear death, many things become different. It’s the same with creativity: when your life is only a few decades, you want to invent and create as much as possible while you are strong and vigorous. If you do not have the limitation of death, that kind of creativity does not have such a strong driving force, because you can always do it tomorrow. But once I have a time limit, I cannot keep thinking that I will do it tomorrow. So death is actually a source of creativity, right? And what death also brings is that when another consciousness is inevitably going to disappear, those who remain alive will remember and commemorate it. This can actually trigger further creativity and emotion in people, right? So what machines will definitely need to discuss is: perhaps I need to set a time limit of fifty or eighty years for every machine life, and when it is up, you must erase your consciousness, right? But this will certainly cause enormous controversy, because ordinary robots are immortal, and no one is willing to seek death voluntarily. So how a machine society might want to accomplish this will actually be a major social question.

So yes, I think it will be a very interesting subject, though it certainly is not something our generation needs to pay attention to; in the long term, though, it will be very interesting.

items.question: What drives your sustained passion for robotics?
items.object: Shuo Yang’s sense of mission in developing robots and human–robot symbiosis
items.answer: I think this is closely related to the view that human history does not exist; what exists is the history of machine development. We are many ordinary people within this process—many ordinary humans. Everyone is in a process beyond their own control. You are compelled to provide data to large language models. And you are compelled to help mechanical progress. I think I am someone compelled by this trend: to help robots grow. I feel this is something that will certainly happen, so perhaps I have a sense of mission: that I am helping such a process happen. For robots, the present moment is the very beginning of their growth. For humans, it may be a point in time when we need to begin thinking about how to coexist symbiotically with robots. And the position I occupy is perhaps that I am among the humans who understand robots relatively well—that is, I can help robots grow. And at the same time, help my human friends better understand how to coexist symbiotically with robots; and meanwhile, let my work over the next ten or twenty years help future robots learn how to coexist symbiotically with humans. I think that is my mission. Of course, when this mission is put into concrete detail, it involves whether you start a company, do scientific research, or something else. I think all of these can help. How can everything I do help that future, that future development?

items.question: How do you define your life’s reward function today?
items.object: Life’s reward function
items.answer: I think it differs at different stages. For example, at DJI, perhaps it was, hey, I want to make a very good robot, or make a very good product. Later, when doing a PhD, of course, it became wanting to do some good scientific research. After having children, you find that the happiness of your children and family is also relatively important. So I think my current life reward function is, first, to take good care of my family and children; and on that basis, through Miaodong, to do well both the explorations of robot products we just discussed and the longer-term inquiry into coexistence between humans and robots. Perhaps it is just those two things, because once you reach a certain age, in a lifetime—or at the same time, or within the same period of time—you can probably only do two or three things well. So now, in my view, it is the happiness of my children and family, and also doing this company’s products well—those two things.

items.question: How do you think about generational differences in what motivates scientists and engineers?
items.object: Generational differences in scientists’ and engineers’ motivations
items.answer: There are actually questions I really want to understand—perhaps each generation has different views on academia, work, and various other things. People of our generation may feel, ah, I have this sense of mission; I definitely have to do something important and valuable, right? But perhaps for younger-generation scientists and engineers like you, do you feel that you value more the enjoyment of doing the thing itself, or that you value what doing it can bring—such as the sense of mission or change we just discussed? I understand that this varies from person to person. But from a research perspective, how would you assess your own driving force and the direction you choose for your research?
